steps.title: Compute neural-network gradients with automatic differentiation

blocks.text: Use the chain-rule reference to check autograd, not just the existence of a gradient.

Autograd builds a computation graph from tensor operations, then applies the chain rule to differentiate its scalar output. Mark trainable leaves with requires_grad=True. Form the supplied scalar loss and call loss.backward(); inspect .grad on each leaf parameter. Clear old gradients before a fresh reference comparison: backward accumulates into .grad.

For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D. Compare the computed gradients to the matrix-shaped chain-rule reference with explicit relative and absolute tolerances. Test valid, boundary and failure fixtures with assert predicates. A false predicate raises AssertionError in ordinary non-optimized execution.

blocks.code:
import torch

W = supplied_W.clone().requires_grad_(True)
b = supplied_b.clone().requires_grad_(True)
W.grad = None
b.grad = None
Z = X @ W + b
loss = supplied_scalar_loss(Z, targets)
loss.backward()
# D is the supplied scalar-loss derivative, including its reduction.
reference_W = X.T @ D
reference_b = D.sum(dim=0)
assert W.grad.shape == reference_W.shape
assert b.grad.shape == reference_b.shape
assert torch.allclose(W.grad, reference_W, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
assert torch.allclose(b.grad, reference_b, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)

steps.title: Compute neural-network gradients with automatic differentiation

blocks.text: Take X=[[1, 2], [3, 4]] and the supplied derivative D=[[0.1], [0.2]] for Z=XW+b. The weight-gradient reference is X.T @ D = [[0.7], [1.0]], and the bias-gradient reference is [0.3]. Any loss reduction is already included in D; dividing again would change the reference. Set trainable leaf tensors to require gradients, form the scalar loss and call backward. Inspect .grad before clearing it, and compare shapes and values under explicit tolerances. For a fresh computation, clear the old gradients first because backward accumulates.
Include a failure fixture whose gradient differs from the declared reference, not only a successful call.

segments.label: Trace a scalar tensor computation and inspect its gradient
segments.summary: PyTorch tracks operations on a tensor when requires_grad=True. Starting with a three-element tensor x, the demonstration forms y = x + 2, multiplies y by itself and by 2, and takes the mean to produce a scalar. Each tracked operation contributes to a computation graph and has an associated gradient function. Calling backward() on the scalar computes its derivative with respect to x and stores the result in x.grad. Repeating the construction without enabling gradient tracking leads to an error when backward() is called. The explanation connects differentiation through the graph to the chain rule: local derivatives are combined to obtain the final gradient. Because the output is scalar, this backward() call needs no explicit gradient argument.

blocks.group_title: How autograd carries derivatives through a computation graph

bridge.before: Watch how tracked operations connect a tensor to a scalar output and how backward() populates its gradient. The clip uses “computational graph”; Devspace calls this a computation graph.
bridge.after: The clip demonstrates the mechanism, not the complete parameter-verification contract. The text adds the supplied-loss leaf-parameter workflow, gradient clearing, matrix references, explicit tolerances, and valid, boundary, and failure assertions.

steps.title: Apply: Verify parameter gradients against the corresponding matrix-shaped derivative reference.

public.prompt: Review gradient checks for X=[[1, 2], [3, 4]], D=[[0.1], [0.2]] and Z=XW+b. D already includes the scalar-loss reduction. The supplied tolerance is rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8. Valid and zero-D boundary references must pass; a deliberately perturbed reference must fail. Sort every excerpt into Supported (all stated contract claims hold) or Defective (at least one stated claim violates the contract). Each excerpt is independent; comments describe recorded fixture evidence.

items.text:
# Trainable leaf W and b have requires_grad=True.
W.grad = None; b.grad = None
loss = supplied_scalar_loss(X @ W + b)
loss.backward()
assert torch.allclose(W.grad, X.T @ D, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8)
assert torch.allclose(b.grad, D.sum(dim=0), rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-8)
# Observed gradient shapes: (2, 1), (1,); references: [[0.7], [1.0]], [0.3].
# Valid and zero-D cases pass. A perturbed reference raises AssertionError.

# The same scalar loss is backpropagated twice without clearing W.grad or b.grad.
# Compare the second accumulated gradients against the one-pass reference.

reference_W = (X.T @ D) / 2
reference_b = D.sum(dim=0) / 2
# Claim: the extra division is required by mean reduction.

e1.message: Fresh leaf gradients are compared with both correctly shaped references under explicit tolerances, including boundary and rejection checks.

e2.message: Backward accumulates gradients, so this is not a fresh single-pass comparison.

e3.message: D already carries the reduction; applying it again produces a different reference.

blocks.text: Choose the output and target contract before choosing the scalar objective.

The scalar objective compares outputs with their corresponding targets. First establish the loss's input contract. CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C). For MSELoss, inputs and targets must share a shape. Mean reduction averages the squared elementwise differences.

blocks.code:
from torch import nn

# Class indices: raw logits (N, C), long targets (N,), indices in [0, C).
class_loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(class_logits, class_indices)
# Numerical targets: same shape as outputs.
regression_loss = nn.MSELoss(reduction="mean")(outputs, numeric_targets)
# Binary targets: same shape, values in [0, 1], raw logits as inputs.
binary_loss = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(reduction="mean")(binary_logits, binary_targets)

mse_D = 2 * (outputs - numeric_targets) / outputs.numel()
binary_D = (binary_logits.sigmoid() - binary_targets) / binary_logits.numel()
class_D = (class_logits.softmax(dim=1) - one_hot_targets) / class_logits.shape[0]

blocks.text: BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs. For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target. For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

For an unweighted mean squared-error fixture with outputs [2, 4] and targets [1, 2], the loss is (1²+2²)/2 = 2.5 and output derivatives are [1, 2]. For a binary-logit fixture with one logit 0 and target 1, sigmoid(0)=0.5, so the supplied mean-logit derivative is −0.5. For target 1, decreasing the logit increases loss, while increasing it decreases loss. For a class-index task with three classes, verify logits width 3 and long target indices in [0, 3); use the stated softmax-minus-one-hot reference with its sample-count reduction.
These are distinct output contracts, not interchangeable wrappers around arbitrary tensors.
Loss names do not repair incompatible shapes or representations. Logits, class indices and same-shaped numerical targets have different contracts.

steps.title: Configure a baseline optimizer and learning rate

blocks.text: Give plain SGD the trainable parameters and verify one current-gradient update.

Pass the model's trainable parameters to torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=declared_learning_rate). For plain SGD without momentum, weight decay or other modifications, the parameter update is parameter_new = parameter_old − learning_rate × gradient. Apply the current update in order: optimizer.zero_grad() clears old gradients, loss.backward() computes gradients, and optimizer.step() updates parameters.

Check one deterministic fixture update against the declared plain-SGD equation, without extending that rule to every optimizer. Test valid, boundary and failure fixtures with assert predicates. A false predicate raises AssertionError in ordinary non-optimized execution.

before.code:
import torch
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = loss_fn(model(features), targets)
loss.backward()
before = [p.detach().clone() for p in model.parameters()]
gradients = [p.grad.detach().clone() for p in model.parameters()]

after.code:
optimizer.step()
for p, old, gradient in zip(model.parameters(), before, gradients):
    expected = old - learning_rate * gradient
    assert torch.allclose(p.detach(), expected, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)

steps.title: Configure a baseline optimizer and learning rate

blocks.text: For plain SGD with no momentum, weight decay or other modifications, let a parameter be 2, its current gradient 3 and learning rate 0.1. The reference new value is 2 − 0.1 × 3 = 1.7, with change −0.3. Clear old gradients, compute backward and then step. Retain the before and after values and compare their difference with the reference under declared tolerances. Initialize the optimizer with model.parameters() so it acts on the supplied trainable model parameters.

A fixture that calls backward but never step would produce a gradient without this parameter update. Keep the plain-SGD restrictions visible so this arithmetic is not mistaken for the update rule of every optimizer.

optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
# Snapshot parameter_before and current gradient before step.
optimizer.step()
# Assert parameter_after == 1.7 and change == -0.3 within supplied tolerances.
# Separate lr=0 boundary asserts parameter_after == 2.
# Deliberately incorrect expected update raises AssertionError.

optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.zero_grad()
optimizer.step()
# Expect the supplied nonzero current-gradient update.

optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(unrelated_parameters, lr=0.1)
# unrelated_parameters are not any trainable model parameters.
# Claim: this verifies the model parameter update.
